title: Nvidia's Best Quarter Ever, and a 12x Multiple
dek: The market isn't doubting $60 billion in net income — it's betting competition is coming. The most profitable quarter in history paired with the cheapest valuation in history is the most counterintuitive thing in this episode.
why: The first half hour is hard data on Nvidia and SaaS; the middle section on US debt and long-end rates is the densest stretch; the last twenty minutes, breaking down the cost of a cancer vaccine, is worth listening to on its own.
who: Investors and founders watching AI compute and SaaS valuations, plus macro traders trying to get straight on US long-end rates and fiscal constraints.
skip: The Ukraine war segment (1:17:53) and the AI writing disclosure fight (1:01:39) can be skipped.

points.h: The best earnings ever come with the cheapest valuation ever
points.body: Nvidia did $96.2 billion in revenue this quarter, more than double year over year, against Wall Street expectations of just $92 billion; more important is the guidance — 70% growth next year, when the market had expected only 45%. Net income of $60 billion makes it the most profitable core-business quarter of any public company in history. Yet even after the stock rose 8% that day, Nvidia trades at just 12 times earnings. The reason isn't that the market disbelieves the numbers — it's that the market believes competition is coming. That combination is the most counterintuitive thing in this episode: the strongest earnings ever, paired with the cheapest valuation ever.

points.h: Stage two of AI is giving the brain hands and eyes
points.body: Chamath splits AI into stages: stage one is the model, essentially a brain; stage two is the harness, meaning agents, essentially giving that brain eyes, hands, a notepad and a keyboard. But he judges stage two isn't enough — what enterprises are really missing is making that autonomous agent more informed and more contextual, so it can actually do the work of a lawyer, a support rep, a salesperson. Whoever owns that context owns the next stage. That's the underlying logic behind his May call that Salesforce was oversold and his insistence on staying long.

Benioff himself raised an underrated point: Salesforce contains a lot of ‘trap value’ — the platform's features are so vast that ordinary users can never find them, but an agent can. The agent will proactively tell the user ‘I see these actions in Salesforce that match what you asked for, want me to run them’, and once the user clicks ‘always allow’, the agent can unlock the full power of Salesforce. That means enterprises no longer need to hire a fleet of expensive consultants to figure Salesforce out. Freeberg's read: Benioff knew that wiring Salesforce into Claude carried disintermediation risk and still handed over the customer relationship, because he knows what customers want is to build agents inside AI and let those agents run across every SaaS platform.

points.h: The SaaS apocalypse is a product of naive extrapolation
points.body: Freeberg reduces this whole narrative cycle to one error: naive extrapolation. The SaaS apocalypse argument runs ‘AI agents will write code, therefore all software goes to zero’; the jobs apocalypse argument runs ‘AI can do knowledge work, therefore all knowledge workers lose their jobs’. Both ignore that people can turn around and use the tools. His conclusion is blunt: those who adopt the technology live, those who don't die. He also notes that Leopold's SaaS short may not be a judgment problem but a leverage problem — to get enough leverage, you can only short the most liquid large caps.

points.h: Nvidia is grabbing open source's distribution layer
points.body: Nvidia reportedly acquired Hugging Face for $12 billion and did an acqui-hire of Poolside for $6 billion, roughly $20 billion combined, less than 1% of Nvidia's market cap. Chamath reads this as Jensen's counterpunch after being provoked by Sam Altman's AMD deal and by in-house inference chips — he wants to own the distribution layer for open source. The bigger judgment is that the boundary between customer and supplier is melting: hyperscalers build their own chips, so Nvidia builds its own models, runs a cloud, serves APIs — eventually every company will do everything.

points.h: Bessent can't save the long end
points.body: Over the next 12 months the US federal government has to refinance $10 trillion of maturing debt, which means going back to the Treasury market to sell new bonds and borrow new money, and borrowing new money costs more, which makes the deficit bigger. So the speaker argues Bessent cannot materially affect the long end no matter what he does — the most buying he can muster is $1 trillion, while he still has to sell $10 trillion. The point of Druck's memo isn't prediction, it's cover for Bessent: push responsibility back onto Congress and the White House, and say this isn't the Treasury secretary's job — it's the people who control the budget who have to cut spending.

points.h: 30-year at 6% is where the death spiral starts
points.body: The speaker's threshold call: if you see the 30-year hit 6%, that's the start of the death spiral. Not an immediate explosion, no reason to panic, but the beginning of extreme pain, and that pain lasts for years. The only fix is getting the budget under control, and that's an act of Congress, and it has to happen, this year or next, it's only a matter of time. Sacks adds that no one controls spending: 435 representatives and 100 senators each have a vote, plus the president, and no single person controls spending — the power of the purse originates in the House, and the president has no line item veto.

points.h: The cancer vaccine is a process, not a new drug
points.body: Moderna went from a $20 billion market cap to $60 billion in two weeks on positive data for a so-called cancer vaccine. But Freeberg points out this neo antigen immunotherapy has existed since the late 1990s: take a tumor sample, sequence its DNA, find the mutation sequences unique to that cancer, then build proteins or mRNA from them and inject them to activate immune cells to attack. Melanoma is the biggest target because UV-induced mutations are distinctive enough. It's more like a process than a traditional drug, and the process is customized per person. What bothers him most is that everyone treats this as a one-of-a-kind breakthrough — people have already gone to Montana, printed peptides from their own cancer sequences, made their own neo antigens, injected them and been cured; today you can pay $50,000 to have it done, lots of clinics do it, and it isn't an FDA-approved drug — while Moderna plans to charge $500,000 for the same process.
